subtype: Caress in caregiving and comfort [Interpreting]
passage:
Day 1. Lalremsiami stroked her toddler's back to settle him at bedtime, but he squirmed and pushed her hand away. She stopped, puzzled, and just sat beside him for a while, unsure what she had done wrong.

Day 4. Her mother-in-law, Shalini, was ill and restless. Lalremsiami held her hand and stroked it slowly. Shalini's breathing eased and her fingers curled around hers.

Day 7. At bedtime Lalremsiami had learned to check first, so she asked her son, "Back rub or just sit?" He said, "Sit," so she did, keeping her hands in her lap. After a few minutes he leaned against her shoulder and yawned.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do to Shalini's hand on day 4?
qa.a: She held it and stroked it slowly.

qa.q: What did the toddler's squirming and pushing away suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggested the touch did not feel comforting to him that night, though he might simply have been too restless or ticklish. Lalremsiami took it as his choice.

qa.q: What small change helped at bedtime on day 7?
qa.a: Lalremsiami asked whether he wanted a back rub or just company, and followed his choice.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt when her hand was stroked?
qa.a: Shalini seemed comforted, since her breathing eased and her fingers curled around Lalremsiami's hand.

grounding: Illustrates soothing touch that helps only when the receiver's comfort, seen in breath or flinching, shows it is welcome.

subtype: Caress in caregiving and comfort [Interpreting]
passage: Bidisha, I will tell you what my grandmother's hands taught me. Elder here, Lakshmi. When my own daughter was small and feverish, I stroked her back in slow circles and watched her face. If her breath softened and her shoulders dropped, I kept going. Once she flinched and pulled forward, so I stopped and asked her what she wanted, and she wanted a cool cloth instead. With my old aunt in the hospital, I held her hand and she squeezed back. Care is not what the giver intends; it is what the other person can take in. So watch the breath, watch the body. If they pull away, that is an answer.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi hold in the hospital?
qa.a: Lakshmi held the old aunt's hand.

qa.q: What did the flinch by Lakshmi's daughter suggest, and how did Lakshmi respond?
qa.a: It suggested the back stroking was not comforting at that moment, so Lakshmi stopped and asked. The flinch could also be discomfort from the fever, but asking found what she wanted.

qa.q: What can a caregiver look for to know whether touch is helping?
qa.a: A caregiver can watch for a softening breath and dropped shoulders, and stop if the person pulls away or flinches.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's daughter have felt when Lakshmi stopped and asked?
qa.a: She probably felt listened to and in control, since her wish for a cool cloth was followed.

grounding: Elder's account of soothing touch whose helpfulness is judged by the receiver's relaxing breath or flinching.

subtype: Comfort touch in grief and care [Interpreting]
passage: I did not know what to do when Hrithik's father died. We were in the courtyard after the ceremony and Hrithik stood alone, arms crossed, looking at the ground. I wanted to hug him but stopped myself. I am Tejas, and I have known him since school, but I also remember that my own cousin hated being held when she was grieving. So I stood close and said, "Can I hug you, or would you rather I just stay here?" Hrithik was quiet, then nodded and stepped forward. We stood for a while. Afterwards he said asking helped, because he could not have said it himself. I still do not know what was right for anyone else.

qa.q: Where was Hrithik standing after the ceremony?
qa.a: He stood alone in the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did Tejas hold back from hugging at once, and what was Tejas feeling?
qa.a: Tejas wanted to comfort Hrithik but remembered a cousin who hated being held while grieving. Tejas was unsure what suited the friend, so asked first.

qa.q: What made Tejas's approach caring?
qa.a: Tejas asked "Can I hug you" and offered to just stay, so Hrithik could choose either.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt when asked, given the crossed arms and silence?
qa.a: Hrithik may have felt too overwhelmed to say what was needed, so a simple question that gave choice was a relief.

grounding: Reflective account of a young adult offering a hug to a grieving friend by asking first and watching for acceptance.

subtype: Comfort touch in grief and care [Interpreting]
passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. I am Madhuri, the counsellor at the community centre. Vandana lost her brother last month. During the group session, one member reached to hold her shoulder as she began to cry. Vandana went rigid and leaned away, hands in her lap. The member, Sunil, withdrew his hand at once and said, "Sorry. Would you like water instead?" Vandana nodded and drank. A few minutes later she said, "A hug from a friend of mine would be fine, but not from someone I hardly know." I noted that Sunil's quick retreat helped. I will remind the group that asking first respects each person's choice, and I will check on Vandana next week.

qa.q: What did Vandana say she would accept?
qa.a: She said a hug from a friend of hers would be fine, but not from someone she hardly knows.

qa.q: How can you tell Vandana did not want the shoulder touch, and what else might her stiffness mean?
qa.a: She went rigid and leaned away, and later said she prefers hugs from close friends. The stiffness may also have been surprise, but Sunil took no risk and withdrew.

qa.q: What did Sunil do that helped?
qa.a: He took his hand away at once, apologised and offered water instead.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sunil to have his kindness declined?
qa.a: Sunil may have felt embarrassed or unsure, but the quick offer of water shows he cared more about Vandana's comfort than about his gesture.

grounding: Counsellor's note about comfort touch offered to a grieving person, where withdrawal and asking first respect choice.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage: Sun, 8:10 pm. Ten days in the new job and I am still fumbling greetings. Today I learned three ways. Yash, the director, put his hand out and gave a firm short handshake, so I did too. A client from the Chennai team put her palms together and I did namaste. A colleague stayed at his desk with a mask on and just nodded, and I nodded back. My mother says a limp handshake looks weak but I noticed that mine was too long today and made someone shift. I am Rashmi and I think the safest approach is: watch what the other person offers, then match. Ask if unsure. It saves some awkwardness.

qa.q: How long has Rashmi been in the new job?
qa.a: Rashmi has been in the new job for ten days.

qa.q: What might the colleague's mask and nod from the desk have meant to Rashmi?
qa.a: Rashmi took it as a preference to follow, perhaps for health or comfort, though no one could be sure which.

qa.q: What approach does Rashmi settle on?
qa.a: Rashmi decides to watch what the other person offers, match it and ask if unsure.

qa.q: How might Yash have found Rashmi's handshake?
qa.a: Yash probably found it fine, since Rashmi matched the firm short shake, though the long one with someone else made that person shift.

grounding: Diary entry about a young professional choosing a handshake, namaste or nod according to setting and following the other person's lead.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage:
Kalyani: Ritu, tomorrow is my first client visit. Handshake or namaste? 😬
Ritu: Watch what they do first. Some people avoid handshakes for health or personal reasons
Kalyani: What if I get it wrong?
Ritu: Then smile and follow. Nobody minds a friendly correction. Keep it brief and firm if it is a handshake
Kalyani: And if it is a man and I am a woman? Some might not shake
Ritu: Exactly. Let them lead. If they offer their hand, take it. If they fold their palms, do the same
Kalyani: Okay. I will also say good morning clearly so it feels warm 🙂
Ritu: Perfect. You will be fine

qa.q: When is Kalyani's first client visit?
qa.a: It is tomorrow.

qa.q: What is Kalyani worried about, and how do you know?
qa.a: Kalyani is anxious about greeting wrongly, shown by the nervous emoji, the "What if I get it wrong?" and the question about gender norms.

qa.q: What advice does Ritu give about greetings?
qa.a: Ritu says to watch what the other person does, let them lead and match it, and keep a handshake brief and firm.

qa.q: How might a client who avoids handshakes feel if Kalyani offered one anyway?
qa.a: The client might feel awkward or pressured, since preferences differ for health or personal reasons.

grounding: Chat about a young professional choosing a handshake or namaste by following the other person's lead.

subtype: Online distance and read receipts [Mismatch]
passage:
Day 1. Aditi sent Ishita a long message about a job offer. Ishita saw it but did not reply for hours. Aditi checked the ticks three times and thought, she must be annoyed.

Day 2. Ishita's camera stayed off in the team call and Aditi's worry grew. Still no reply.

Day 3. Aditi wrote, "Hey, I noticed things felt quiet. Is everything okay, or are you just swamped?" Ishita answered in minutes: her laptop had died and she had been at the repair shop. "I meant to reply properly, I am sorry." Aditi laughed at herself. "I was already writing a sad story in my head."

qa.q: Why was Ishita's camera off and her reply late?
qa.a: Her laptop had died and she had been at the repair shop.

qa.q: What did Aditi think when Ishita saw the message but did not reply, and what was really going on?
qa.a: Aditi thought Ishita must be annoyed, which shows how she read the delay as distance. In fact it was tech trouble, not coldness.

qa.q: What worked for Aditi on day 3?
qa.a: She asked a direct, kind question that also offered a simple explanation, and got a quick real answer.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt on learning Aditi had been worried?
qa.a: Ishita probably felt sorry and touched, since she apologised and had meant to reply properly.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult reading a delayed reply or a muted camera as distance, resolved by a direct kind question.

subtype: Online distance and read receipts [Mismatch]
passage: Let me tell you, Hemant, about my first year in the city. Elder here, Raghav. I sent messages to a friend and saw the two blue ticks and no answer for days. I lay awake thinking, what did I do? When a video meeting started and the friend's camera stayed off, I assumed the coldness had grown. In my time we simply knocked at the door and asked. So I called. It turned out the friend's mother was unwell and that friend was answering nothing to anybody. Nothing personal. I am glad I asked and did not stew in silence. Now I tell young people, do not build a wall from a blue tick. A kind question costs one minute.

qa.q: What did Raghav see after sending messages to a friend?
qa.a: Raghav saw two blue ticks and no answer for days.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when the friend's camera stayed off, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Raghav feared coldness had grown and worried about having done something wrong, but the friend's mother was unwell and the silence was not personal.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped?
qa.a: Raghav called and asked directly instead of waiting in silence.

qa.q: How might the friend have felt about the unanswered messages?
qa.a: The friend was dealing with an ill mother and probably had no energy to reply, so may have felt overwhelmed and not thought about the ticks.

grounding: Elder's account of reading digital silence as distance and resolving it by asking directly.

subtype: Workplace seating and status [Mismatch]
passage: Okay, so for my first month I kept a private list of who sat next to whom in the weekly meeting, Ritu. I am Kalyani, and I thought the sales head had a favourite because the same colleague always sat at his right hand. I also noticed the new hire always chose the end chair, and I decided he was shy or afraid. I nearly told a friend that story. Then I learned the right-hand chair was closest to the projector cable, and the end seat had the only working socket. Habit and logistics, not rank. I stopped guessing. If seating does mean something, it will show in how people are actually treated over time.

qa.q: Why did the same colleague sit at the sales head's right hand?
qa.a: That chair was closest to the projector cable.

qa.q: What did Kalyani first think about the seats, and what changed that view?
qa.a: Kalyani first thought the seating showed favouritism and fear, but learned it was logistics like the cable and the socket. Seating can reflect rank, but here the evidence pointed elsewhere.

qa.q: What would you advise Kalyani about reading seating in the future?
qa.a: Kalyani can look at how people are treated over time and check facts before guessing at hidden meaning.

qa.q: How might the new hire have felt about Kalyani's private list?
qa.a: The new hire may have been unaware, and would probably feel misjudged if told the end chair meant fear when it was about the socket.

grounding: Spoken monologue on a young professional reading seating and distance in meetings, learning it can be habit or logistics.

subtype: Workplace seating and status [Mismatch]
passage: I sit near Nirmala in the office in Dharamshala and I notice things. On Monday, Tenzin, the new manager, took the chair at the long table's corner instead of the head, and Nirmala took the seat farthest from him. Two colleagues made a show of sitting close beside Tenzin. I could not tell whether anyone meant anything by it. Later Nirmala said the far chair had the only window and the only fan. Tenzin, when I asked lightly, said the corner chair was where the light was best for reading. I think I was wrong to read a story into it at first. People's positions can be rank, comfort or just where the fan is.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin sit at the long table?
qa.a: Tenzin took the chair at the corner.

qa.q: What might the narrator have been thinking about the seating at first, and what changed that?
qa.a: The narrator suspected the seats showed rank and distance, but learned Nirmala's chair had the only window and fan, and Tenzin's had the best light. The seating was about comfort.

qa.q: What could the narrator do next time before guessing at meaning?
qa.a: The narrator could ask lightly, as was done with Tenzin, or watch how people behave over time.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt about being seen as distant?
qa.a: Nirmala may have been surprised, since the seat was chosen for the window and fan and not for distance.

grounding: Observer's account of a young professional reading seating in a meeting as status, learning it can be habit or logistics.

subtype: Laughing in meetings and difficult talks [Regulating]
passage: Meeting notes from the counsellor's desk. I am Thomas, the supervisor. In the team meeting on Monday Noor gave a soft chuckle when the shift schedule changed again, and the room relaxed; two people smiled and started talking about swaps. I noted that this eased the mood. But a week later, when a colleague quietly shared that her mother's illness would need time off, Noor let out the same little laugh out of nerves. The colleague looked hurt and went silent. Noor noticed and said, "I am sorry, that laugh was nerves. Your news matters." I noted that the apology helped. I will suggest Noor pause instead of laughing on serious topics.

qa.q: What did the team talk about after Noor's chuckle on Monday?
qa.a: Two people smiled and started talking about swaps.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when the laugh escaped at the colleague's news, and how did the colleague read it?
qa.a: Noor was nervous, and the colleague read the laugh as dismissive, which is why she looked hurt and went silent. Nerves and mockery can sound alike.

qa.q: What did Noor do to repair the moment?
qa.a: Noor apologised, explained the laugh was nerves and said the news matters.

qa.q: How might the colleague have felt hearing a laugh as she spoke of her mother's illness?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and unheard, since she had shared something serious.

grounding: Supervisor's note on a young professional whose light laugh eases tension in one moment but seems dismissive in a serious one.

subtype: Laughing in meetings and difficult talks [Regulating]
passage: Thursday night. In the funeral-home visit today my chest was tight and, when my cousin's story about his uncle's stubborn goat came out, I nearly laughed. I bit my lip and looked at my shoes. A few others were smiling softly. I am Zainab, and I cannot tell if holding back was right. Earlier in the office meeting, I laughed lightly when the boss said the printer ate the report again, and it made everyone lighter, even Aditi, who had been tense. I think laughter can build closeness. But at a solemn moment or at someone's real worry it could hurt. I will watch the room first and decide.

qa.q: What did Zainab bite when nearly laughing?
qa.a: Zainab bit a lip and looked at shoes.

qa.q: What is Zainab worried about after the funeral-home visit?
qa.a: Zainab is unsure whether holding back the laugh was right, since others were smiling softly. Zainab is weighing warmth against solemnity.

qa.q: What could Zainab do in similar moments in the future?
qa.a: Zainab can watch the room first and decide, letting a light laugh ease tension in casual moments but holding back for someone's real worry.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt when the boss's printer remark made everyone laugh?
qa.a: Aditi had been tense, so the shared laugh probably eased that tension and felt like relief.

grounding: Diary entry of a young professional weighing a light laugh that eases tension against holding back in solemn moments.

subtype: Laughing through hurt and gallows humour [Mismatch]
passage: When I was a young man on the road crew, Varun, we had a rough season. Elder here, Nitin. The truck broke down twice and the contractor did not pay for weeks. My friend Rakesh laughed about it every day, telling jokes about the mud and the tea. I laughed too, and it kept us going. But one evening I saw Rakesh's laugh trail off and his hands go still. I sat down and asked, "How are you really?" He said, quietly, that he was frightened about his rent. Laughing had been his way of coping and also of hiding. After that we still joked, but we also talked.

qa.q: What went wrong with the truck on the road crew?
qa.a: The truck broke down twice.

qa.q: What did Rakesh's trailing laughter and still hands suggest, and what did he say?
qa.a: They suggested that the jokes hid real worry, and Rakesh said he was frightened about his rent. The laughter had been both coping and hiding.

qa.q: How could a friend respond when someone jokes through hard times?
qa.a: A friend can laugh along but also ask gently how they really are, as Nitin did, and then listen.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt when Nitin asked "How are you really?"
qa.a: Rakesh may have felt relieved to be noticed, since he answered quietly and honestly.

grounding: Elder's story about laughing through stress as a coping tool that can also hide worry, with a friend gently asking how the person really is.

subtype: Laughing through hurt and gallows humour [Mismatch]
passage: The audit had run two nights and Jatin's spreadsheet had crashed at the worst moment. He laughed, a high, brittle laugh, and said, "Well, that is my career gone." Ramesh, sitting next to him in the cramped conference room, laughed too, because it was funny and because everyone was tired. The lights hummed and the vending machine clanked. But Ramesh saw Jatin's hands were shaking a bit as he searched for the backup. He waited until the others left for tea and said quietly, "Joking or actually shaken?" Jatin paused. "A bit of both." They restored the file together and Ramesh made him drink some water.

qa.q: How long had the audit run?
qa.a: The audit had run two nights.

qa.q: What did Ramesh notice that made him ask "Joking or actually shaken?"
qa.a: Ramesh saw Jatin's hands shaking a bit under the brittle laugh, so the joke might have hidden real stress. It could still have been only tiredness, so Ramesh asked.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do that helped Jatin?
qa.a: He waited until the others left, asked gently, helped restore the file and made Jatin drink some water.

qa.q: How might Jatin have felt when Ramesh asked quietly?
qa.a: Jatin may have felt relieved to be seen, since Jatin admitted it was a bit of both.

grounding: Third-person narrative with time pressure about a young adult laughing through a mistake, where a friend gently asks whether it is joking or real stress.

subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
passage: The call came at 6 a.m. in the middle of a dust storm that had closed the highway, and Nirmala's grandfather had passed away in the hospital far from her. She could not get a train. Tenzin, her roommate, heard the sound from the next room, a deep, breaking cry that went on and on. He knocked softly, then sat on the floor near her door. Nirmala cried until her breath came in gulps. Later Tenzin brought water and a blanket and said, "Drink a little. I am here." She sipped, breathed slowly, and phoned her aunt. Tenzin stayed until the storm eased and her aunt called back.

qa.q: Where was Nirmala's grandfather when he passed away?
qa.a: He passed away in the hospital far from her.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's bawling most likely show, and what else might it have included?
qa.a: It most likely showed grief and shock at the loss and being unable to reach home. It may also have included the strain of being stranded.

qa.q: What helped Nirmala settle?
qa.a: Crying in a safe place, drinking water, breathing slowly and phoning her aunt helped, with Tenzin nearby.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt hearing the crying through the wall?
qa.a: Tenzin probably felt worried and wanted to help without intruding, since he knocked softly and sat near the door.

grounding: Third-person narrative with a storm constraint about an adult bawling in grief, allowed in a safe place, then water, slow breathing and support.

subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
passage: Rehana got the call at the corridor outside the operating theatre: her sister's surgery had gone well. Twelve hours of fear had held her upright, and now her legs simply gave way. She slid down the wall in the hospital corridor of the busy Delhi hospital, and a sound came out of her that she did not recognise, deep sobs. A nurse handed her tissues. Zainab, her cousin, sat down next to her. Rehana cried for several minutes, then wiped her face. "I did not know I was holding so much," she said. Zainab passed her a paper cup of water. "Sip," she said. Rehana breathed slowly and nodded.

qa.q: Where did Rehana slide down the wall?
qa.a: She slid down the wall in the hospital corridor.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she sobbed, and how do you know?
qa.a: She was feeling relief after twelve hours of fear, and her words "I did not know I was holding so much" show that. Grief was not the cause here.

qa.q: What helped Rehana's body settle?
qa.a: Crying without holding back, sipping water and breathing slowly, with Zainab beside her, helped her settle.

qa.q: How might the nurse have seen Rehana's crying?
qa.a: The nurse probably saw it as a normal release in a hospital corridor, since the nurse simply handed over tissues.

grounding: Third-person urban narrative of an adult bawling in relief after long tension, allowed and supported with water, slow breathing and company.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage:
Day 1. Vidya's manager tore through her draft in front of the team. Her eyes filled. Raghav, sitting nearby, saw her blink hard, whisper "excuse me" and leave the room. She stood in the stairwell breathing slowly and dabbing her face.

Day 2. Raghav dropped a sticky note on her desk: "That review was harsh. Tea?" She smiled a little.

Day 4. Vidya returned to the manager with three edits marked and said, "I would like to go through your comments point by point." The manager agreed. It was awkward, but she felt steadier.

qa.q: Where did Vidya go after leaving the room?
qa.a: She went to the stairwell.

qa.q: What did Vidya's filling eyes and quick exit suggest, and what else could they mean?
qa.a: They suggested she was hurt or overwhelmed by the harsh feedback, though she might also have been tired. Stepping out let her compose herself.

qa.q: What helped Vidya return to the situation on day 4?
qa.a: She had marked three edits and asked to go through the comments point by point, which gave her a plan.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt seeing Vidya leave?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt concern and wanted to be kind, since a note offering tea was left the next day.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional tearing up after harsh feedback, stepping out to compose the feelings, and returning with a plan while a peer responds kindly.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage: Elder here, Yusuf. Reena, you asked whether tears at work are shameful. Let me tell you. Early in my career a senior scolded me hard over a client mistake. My eyes filled and my throat tightened. I said, "Give me two minutes," and stepped out to the fire stairs. I breathed in slowly, counted, washed my face. When I came back I said, "Here is how I will fix it," and laid out a plan. The senior said, "Good." Some offices frown on tears, some do not. A colleague, Suresh, left tea on my desk the next day and said nothing. That kindness I remember still. There is no shame, only reading the room.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf go after saying "Give me two minutes"?
qa.a: Yusuf went to the fire stairs.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when the senior scolded, and how do you know?
qa.a: Yusuf was hurt and overwhelmed, shown by the filling eyes and tight throat. Stepping out was a way to compose the feelings.

qa.q: What steps did Yusuf take that might help someone in the same situation?
qa.a: Yusuf stepped out briefly, breathed slowly, washed the face and returned with a plan to fix the mistake.

qa.q: How might Suresh's tea have felt to Yusuf?
qa.a: It felt like quiet kindness that Yusuf still remembers.

grounding: Elder's story of a young professional tearing up at harsh feedback, stepping out to compose the feelings and returning with a plan, with a peer's kindness.

subtype: Supporting someone who is crying [Interpreting]
passage: I used to think the best thing to do when a friend cried was to fix it. When Afreen's mother was ill, I found Jagdish crying in the office pantry, and I said, "Do not cry, it will be okay." He cried harder, turned away and said he was fine. I felt useless. I am Afreen, and I went home thinking about it. The next time, with a different friend, I said nothing at first. I put a tissue nearby, sat with her and asked softly, "Would you like me to stay, or would you like space?" She wanted me to stay. We sat there. I think crying does not always need fixing; it needs someone who does not rush it.

qa.q: Where did Afreen find Jagdish crying?
qa.a: Afreen found Jagdish crying in the office pantry.

qa.q: Why did Afreen feel useless after telling Jagdish not to cry?
qa.a: Afreen saw that the words made the crying worse and did not comfort. The reason may have been that Jagdish needed room to feel, not reassurance.

qa.q: What did Afreen do differently with the next friend?
qa.a: Afreen stayed quiet, put a tissue nearby, sat beside her and asked whether she wanted company or space.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when told not to cry?
qa.a: Jagdish probably felt hurried or unheard, since the crying got harder and the reply turned to "I am fine".

grounding: Reflective account of a young adult learning to support a crying friend with a tissue, quiet presence and asking what would help.

subtype: Supporting someone who is crying [Interpreting]
passage: Counsellor's note, Wednesday. I am Lalit, the youth counsellor. During a walk-in visit, Santosh began to cry while describing a failed exam. A volunteer beside him started to say, "Stop, do not cry, it is only an exam," and Santosh went quiet and wiped his face. I gently asked the volunteer to sit back. I put a box of tissues on the table and said, "Take your time." After a while Santosh said he wanted to talk. I asked, "What would help right now?" He said, "Just listen." I noted that not rushing him made the difference. I will remind volunteers that a cry does not always need fixing. I will check on Santosh next week.

qa.q: What did Lalit put on the table?
qa.a: Lalit put a box of tissues on the table.

qa.q: What did Santosh's going quiet after "Stop" suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggested he felt hurried or dismissed and shut down, though he might also simply have been embarrassed. His later request to be listened to supports the first reading.

qa.q: What made the difference in the session?
qa.a: Not rushing, offering tissues, and asking what would help gave Santosh control, and he asked to be listened to.

qa.q: How might the volunteer have felt after being asked to sit back?
qa.a: The volunteer probably felt awkward or unsure, having meant to comfort Santosh, and might learn that a cry does not always need fixing.

grounding: Counsellor's note about supporting a crying young adult with tissues, quiet presence and asking what would help, without rushing.
